- bandleader | | Instrument | [Drums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_kit "Drum kit") | | Years active | 1961–1997 | Musical artist **Anthony Tillmon Williams** (December 12, 1945 – February 23, 1997)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer)#cite_note-1) was an American [jazz drummer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_drumming "Jazz drumming"). Williams first gained fame as a member of [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s " [Second Great Quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_Quintet#Second_Great_Quintet_(1964%E2%80%9368) "Miles Davis Quintet")", and later pioneered [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") with Davis's group and his own combo, [The Tony Williams Lifetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Williams_Lifetime "The Tony Williams Lifetime").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer)#cite_note-2) In 1970, music critic [Robert Christgau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Christgau "Robert Christgau") described him as "probably the best drummer in the world".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer)#cite_note-3) Williams was inducted into the _[Modern Drummer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Drummer "Modern Drummer")_ Hall of Fame in 1986 and the [Percussive Arts Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percussive_Arts_Society "Percussive Arts Society") Hall of Fame in 1997.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer)#cite_note-4) ## Life and career Williams was born in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"), [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois"), and grew up in [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston"), [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer)#cite_note-drummerworld-5) He was of African, Portuguese, and Chinese descent.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer)#cite_note-drummerworld-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer)#cite_note-6) He studied with drummer [Alan Dawson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Dawson "Alan Dawson") at the age of 11, and began playing professionally at the age of 13 with saxophonist [Sam Rivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Rivers_(jazz_musician) "Sam Rivers (jazz musician)"). Saxophonist [Jackie McLean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_McLean "Jackie McLean") hired Williams when he, Williams, was 16.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer)#cite_note-drummerworld-5)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer)#cite_note-7) As a young drummer, he was influenced by [Max Roach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Roach "Max Roach"), [Art Blakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Blakey "Art Blakey"), [Philly Joe Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philly_Joe_Jones "Philly Joe Jones"), [Roy Haynes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Haynes "Roy Haynes"), [Louis Hayes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Hayes "Louis Hayes"), and [Jimmy Cobb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Cobb "Jimmy Cobb").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer)#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer)#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer)#cite_note-10) At 17, Williams joined [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") in what was later dubbed Davis's [Second Great Quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_Quintet#Second_Great_Quintet_(1964%E2%80%9368) "Miles Davis Quintet")—with saxophonist [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter"), pianist [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), and bassist [Ron Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Carter "Ron Carter"). Davis had been in something of a creative lull, and critics noted the young Tony Williams' playing spurred the others on.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer)#cite_note-fordham-11) Williams was a vital element of the group, called by Davis in his autobiography "the center that the group's sound revolved around".[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer)#cite_note-12) His playing helped redefine the role of the jazz [rhythm section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_section "Rhythm section") through the use of [polyrhythms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyrhythm "Polyrhythm") and [metric modulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_modulation "Metric modulation"). Meanwhile, he recorded his first two albums as a leader for the [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") label: _[Life Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_Time_(Tony_Williams_album) "Life Time (Tony Williams album)")_ (1964) and _[Spring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spring_(Tony_Williams_album) "Spring (Tony Williams album)")_ (1965). He also recorded as a sideman for the label including the classics _[Out to Lunch!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch! "Out to Lunch!")_ with [Eric Dolphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy "Eric Dolphy") and _[Point of Departure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_of_Departure_(Andrew_Hill_album) "Point of Departure (Andrew Hill album)")_ with [Andrew Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Hill_(pianist) "Andrew Hill (pianist)"), both in 1964. In 1969 Williams formed [The Tony Williams Lifetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Williams_Lifetime "The Tony Williams Lifetime"), with [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)") on guitar and [Larry Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Young_(musician) "Larry Young (musician)") on organ.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer)#cite_note-drummerworld-5) Lifetime was a pioneering band of the [fusion movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-rock_fusion "Jazz-rock fusion").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer)#cite_note-LarkinJazz-13) Their first album was [_Emergency!_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album) "Emergency! (album)"). For the album _[Turn It Over](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn_It_Over "Turn It Over")_, the trio was joined by bass guitarist and vocalist [Jack Bruce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Bruce "Jack Bruce"). After several more releases and touring, Lifetime disbanded. In 1975, Williams formed "The New Tony Williams Lifetime", featuring bassist [Tony Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Newton_(American_musician) "Tony Newton (American musician)"), keyboardist [Alan Pasqua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Pasqua "Alan Pasqua") and guitarist [Allan Holdsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allan_Holdsworth "Allan Holdsworth"), who recorded two albums for [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"): _[Believe It](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Believe_It_(album) "Believe It (album)")_ and _[Million Dollar Legs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Million_Dollar_Legs_(album) "Million Dollar Legs (album)")_. In 1976, Williams reunited with his colleagues from the Miles Davis Quintet.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer)#cite_note-drummerworld-5) (Davis himself was in the midst of a six-year hiatus and was "replaced" by trumpeter [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard").) (divorced)​ | | | | Website | [mccoytyner.com](http://mccoytyner.com/) | | | | Relatives | [Jarvis Tyner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jarvis_Tyner "Jarvis Tyner") (brother) | | | Musical artist **Alfred McCoy Tyner** (December 11, 1938–March 6, 2020) was an American [jazz pianist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_piano "Jazz piano") and composer known for his work with the [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") Quartet from 1960 to 1965 and his long solo career afterward.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-1) He was an [NEA Jazz Master](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NEA_Jazz_Masters "NEA Jazz Masters") and a five-time [Grammy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy "Grammy") Award winner. Tyner has been widely imitated and is one of the most recognizable and influential jazz pianists of all time.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-nytdeath-2) ## Early life and education \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=McCoy_Tyner&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")\] Tyner was born on December 11, 1938,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-McCoy_Tyner:_The_Pianist-4) in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), Pennsylvania, United States, the eldest of Jarvis and Beatrice (née Stevenson) Tyner's three children.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-Chinen-5) Tyner was encouraged to study piano by his mother, who had installed a piano at her beauty salon. At the age of 13, he began piano lessons at the [Granoff School of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granoff_School_of_Music "Granoff School of Music"), where he also studied [music theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_theory "Music theory") and [harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony "Harmony"). By the time he was 15 years old, music had become the center of his life.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-NEA-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-7) Tyner's decision to study piano was reinforced when he encountered [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") pianist [Bud Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bud_Powell "Bud Powell"), a neighbor of the Tyner family.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-Collar-8) Another major influence on Tyner's playing was [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk"), whose percussive attacks informed Tyner's style.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-McCoy_Tyner:_The_Pianist-4) During his teens, Tyner led his own group, the Houserockers.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-Heckman-9) When he was 17, Tyner converted to [Ahmadiyya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmadiyya "Ahmadiyya") and changed his name to Suleiman Saud,[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-11) although he continued to perform as "McCoy Tyner".[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-Collar-8) ## Early career and the John Coltrane Quartet \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=McCoy_Tyner&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Early career and the John Coltrane Quartet")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/McCoy_Keystone.jpg/250px-McCoy_Keystone.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:McCoy_Keystone.jpg) Tyner at [Keystone Korner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keystone_Korner "Keystone Korner") in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco"), in March 1981[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/McCoyTynerandRaviColtrane.jpg/250px-McCoyTynerandRaviColtrane.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:McCoyTynerandRaviColtrane.jpg) Tyner with [Ravi Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravi_Coltrane "Ravi Coltrane") at the [Newport Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Jazz_Festival "Newport Jazz Festival") in [Newport, Rhode Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport,_Rhode_Island "Newport, Rhode Island"), in August 2005[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/McCoy_Tyner_04.jpg/250px-McCoy_Tyner_04.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:McCoy_Tyner_04.jpg) Tyner with his quartet at Jazz Alley in [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle"), in April 2012 Tyner began playing professionally in Philadelphia with local artists such as [Lee Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Morgan "Lee Morgan") and [Jimmy Heath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Heath "Jimmy Heath"), participating in the city's modern jazz scene.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-Chinen-5)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-Collar-8) He first met [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"), who eventually became "like a big brother" to Tyner,[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-Milkowski-12) in the summer of 1955. They kept in touch, played together occasionally, and had an understanding that if Coltrane ever formed a group of his own, Tyner would be the pianist.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-13) In 1960, Tyner joined [The Jazztet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jazztet "The Jazztet") led by [Benny Golson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benny_Golson "Benny Golson") and [Art Farmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Farmer "Art Farmer") and recorded on the group's debut album, _[Meet the Jazztet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meet_the_Jazztet "Meet the Jazztet")_. Around the same time, Coltrane left [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s group and formed a quartet of his own, but because he was friends with Golson, he was reluctant to ask Tyner to leave The Jazztet. Encouraged by his wife, Naima, Coltrane eventually asked Tyner what he wanted to do.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-14) After six months with The Jazztet, Tyner joined the John Coltrane Quartet, which then included bassist [Steve Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Davis_(bassist) "Steve Davis (bassist)") and drummer [Elvin Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvin_Jones "Elvin Jones"). Tyner worked with the band during its extended run at the Jazz Gallery, replacing [Steve Kuhn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Kuhn "Steve Kuhn").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-Collar-8)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-15) Reflecting on the situation later, Tyner said: "There were probably some bad feelings at first with the Jazztet, but I think they understood better later on. John's group was where I belonged."[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-16) Coltrane had already recorded Tyner's composition "The Believer" on January 10, 1958, which became the title track of [Prestige Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records "Prestige Records")' 1964 [album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Believer_(John_Coltrane_album) "The Believer (John Coltrane album)") under Coltrane's name.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-17)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner#cite_note-18) [... middle omitted — see footer ...] - He is among the most influential and acclaimed figures in the [history of jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz#Post-war_jazz "Jazz") and 20th-century music. Born and raised in [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina"), Coltrane moved to [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") after high school, where he immersed himself in the local jazz scene, studied music, and served in the [Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy") toward the end of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") before making his professional debut in 1945. Working in the [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") and [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop") idioms early in his career, Coltrane helped pioneer the use of [modes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz "Modal jazz") and was one of the players at the forefront of [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"). He led at least fifty recording sessions and appeared on many albums by other musicians, including trumpeter [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") and pianist [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk"). Over the course of his career, Coltrane's music took on an increasingly spiritual dimension, as exemplified on his most acclaimed album _[A Love Supreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme "A Love Supreme")_ (1965) and others.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane#cite_note-1) Decades after his death, Coltrane remains influential, and he has received numerous posthumous awards, including a [special Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_Special_Citations_and_Awards "Pulitzer Prize Special Citations and Awards"),[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane#cite_note-pulitzer-2) and he was [canonized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonization "Canonization") by the [African Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Orthodox_Church "African Orthodox Church"). His second wife was pianist and harpist [Alice Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Coltrane "Alice Coltrane"). The couple had three children: John Jr. (1964-1982), a bassist;[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane#cite_note-3) [Ravi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravi_Coltrane "Ravi Coltrane") (born 1965), a saxophonist; and Oran (born 1967), a saxophonist, guitarist, drummer, and singer.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane#cite_note-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane#cite_note-6) ## Biography ### 1926–1945: Early life [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/U.S._Naval_Reserve_portrait_of_Johnny_Coltrane_edit.jpg/500px-U.S._Naval_Reserve_portrait_of_Johnny_Coltrane_edit.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:U.S._Naval_Reserve_portrait_of_Johnny_Coltrane_edit.jpg) Coltrane's first recordings were made when he was a sailor. Coltrane was born in his parents' apartment at 200 Hamlet Avenue in [Hamlet, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamlet,_North_Carolina "Hamlet, North Carolina"), on September 23, 1926.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane#cite_note-7) His father was John R. Coltrane[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane#cite_note-8) and his mother was Alice Blair.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane#cite_note-DeVito_et_al.,_p._3-9) He grew up in [High Point, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Point,_North_Carolina "High Point, North Carolina"), and attended [William Penn High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Penn_High_School_(North_Carolina) "William Penn High School (North Carolina)"). While in high school, Coltrane played [clarinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarinet "Clarinet") and [alto horn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor_horn "Tenor horn") in a community band[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane#cite_note-10) before switching to the saxophone, after being influenced by the likes of [Lester Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Young "Lester Young") and [Johnny Hodges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Hodges "Johnny Hodges").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane#cite_note-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane#cite_note-12) Beginning in December 1938, his father, aunt, and grandparents died within a few months of one another, leaving him to be raised by his mother and a close cousin.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane#cite_note-13) In June 1943, shortly after graduating from high school, Coltrane and his family moved to Philadelphia, where he got a job at a [sugar refinery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_refinery "Sugar refinery").
